To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

vertical variability of chlorophyll in a mode-water anticyclone is controlled by a combination of nutrient availability and light availability in its deep layer, which in turn is driven by the vertical nutrient flux in the deep layer that varies with the eddy-induced isopycnal displacement.

the vertical chlorophyll variability within the core of an anticyclonic eddy is caused by the change of nutrient-light interaction, which leads to a shift of phytoplanktons physiology and hence vertical enhancement of chlorophyll in the DCM.

the DCM in a mode water eddy is controlled by the nutrient-light interaction and that the DCM variability is mainly driven by the vertical nutrient flux in the deep layer as a result of eddy-induced isopycnal motion.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how the physical processes control phytoplankton distribution in the deep ocean, with the ultimate goal of understanding the role of the deep ocean in the global carbon cycle and the global climate change.
the physical and biological processes that control the vertical structure of phytoplankon distribution in a stratified eddy.
how the physical environment controls the biological processes and the resulting chlorophyll distributions within the core of an anticyclonic mode-water eddy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the DCM layer is controlled by a complex interplay of vertical mixing, particle settling, and nutrient cycling, and that this interplay is modulated by the eddy-induced isopycnal motion in the deep layer of the eddies.
a DCM layer is formed in the core of the eddy due to nutrient-light interaction, which is driven by the vertical nutrient flux variation in the deep layer.
the observed variability of the DCM layer in the mode-water eddy is controlled by a combination of nutrient-light interactions and vertical fluxes of nutrients in the deep layer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the DCM layer in the core of the modewater eddy is controlled by nutrient availability, and the variability of chlorophyll concentration in the DCM is largely driven by the vertical variability of nutrient fluxes.

the observed DDM variability is largely controlled by the vertical flux of nutrients, which is in turn controlled by the vertical mixing and particle fluxes, while the vertical distribution of chlorophyll is controlled by nutrientlight interaction.
the observed chlorophyll enhancement in the DCM of an eddy is a result of nutrient-light interaction, which in turn is largely driven by isopycnal nutrient fluxes in the deep layer of the eddies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vertical nutrient flux is a key control on DCM formation in stratified eddies, which is consistent with the previous studies on DCMs in the open oceans.

the DCM layer is a sensitive indicator of the vertical structure of the eddy, and thus the vertical variability of chlorophyll concentration in the deep layer is a result of the interplay between the physical and biological processes.
a deep chlorophyll enhancement can be sustained by nutrient recycling within the deep layer and is controlled by the vertical nutrient flux in the DCM.
